title: Sita sent away
hookLine: gossip reaches the king, and Sita is sent into the forest
carry: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned
last: BHAKTI KEEPS GOD IN THE HEART.

lines: A CROWNING, AND A JUST REIGN.
cards: Many recitations of the Ramayana stop at the crowning, with a pearl necklace and a just reign. But the Ramayana as it has come down has one more book.
It's called the Uttara Kanda, the later book, or the book that comes after. It gets six days here, and its argument stays open, the way the tradition has left it.
Because this book takes the couple who just came home, and pulls them apart again.

teach.b: Uttara means later; kanda, a section of the poem. The seventh book of Valmiki's Ramayana: many scholars think it was added later; many in the tradition receive it as his own. It comes back to Ayodhya.
Rama rules; Sita is pregnant; they walk in the palace gardens.
One day Rama asks a companion named Bhadra what the people say about him. Bhadra hesitates, then tells him. They praise the war.
But some say: how can the king take back a wife who lived in Ravana's house? If the king allows it, we'll have to put up with it from our own wives. Rama calls his brothers.
He has decided: Sita will be taken to the forest near the sage Valmiki's hermitage, and left there. He forbids them to argue. Once again it falls to Lakshmana, with the charioteer Sumantra.
Sita thinks she's going to visit the hermits, as she had asked. At the Ganga, Lakshmana breaks down and tells her the truth.
The poem shows Rama in grief and Sita blameless, both at once. This is the hardest scene in the Ramayana, and Hindus have argued with it for centuries.
The Mahabharata says more than once that dharma is subtle: a king's duty to his people and a husband's duty to his wife can pull apart. Some defend Rama's choice as a king's sacrifice.

The playwright Bhavabhuti built a whole drama on his grief. Women's songs in many Indian languages take Sita's side. Many teachers say wrestling with this scene isn't disrespect; it's part of the tradition.

how: Hindu families and teachers handle the Uttara Kanda in different ways: some recite it in full, many traditional readings stop at the coronation, and many retellings tell Sita's exile with open grief and debate.

s: Hindu tradition forbids questioning Rama's choice
poets, teachers and women's songs have argued over it for centuries; the Mahabharata calls dharma subtle.
the Uttara Kanda is the Ramayana's seventh book
it comes after the war book; many scholars think it was added later, while many in the tradition receive it as Valmiki's own.
Sita knows from the start that she's being sent away
she thinks it's a visit to the hermits. Lakshmana tells her at the Ganga.

games.q: at a family party, an auntie says Rama was wrong to send Sita away, and an uncle says no one can question Rama. by the tradition, what fits?
o: the uncle: questioning Rama is disrespect.
both can speak: Hindus have argued this scene for centuries, and dharma is subtle.
the auntie: this one scene makes the whole Ramayana wrong.
games.why: Valmiki shows Rama grieving and Sita blameless; poets, teachers and women's songs have argued it ever since. the tradition keeps the question open.

practice: There's an old Hindu word for this kind of practice: manana, turning a teaching over in your mind after you've heard it. Picture Rama, alone, deciding. Then Sita, on the far bank.
Don't settle who was right. Notice where your sympathy goes, and let it stay with both. If you'd like to pray, ask for clear seeing; if not, just breathe and hold the question.

wordCard.voice: Uttara Kanda. The Ramayana's seventh book, which opens, after the happy ending, with gossip, a king's decision, and Sita sent into the forest.

orig.note: Sanskrit uttarakāṇḍa: uttara (later, after) + kāṇḍa (section). the seventh book of Valmiki's Ramayana.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned. Both griefs are in the poem. Tomorrow, two boys in a hermitage. See you then.
